name: Smart scale
lead: A smart scale is a bathroom scale that records body weight with load cells and sends the reading, usually by Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, to a phone app or web dashboard. Many models also report an estimated body-fat percentage and related figures, typically derived from bioelectrical impedance, in which a small electrical current is passed through the feet. In appearance-focused and physique communities the device is used mainly to log weight trends during cutting, bulking and recomposition phases.

Research on the category has mostly used connected scales as a data-collection tool inside weight-management trials rather than testing the scale as a product in its own right. In those studies, daily or frequent self-weighing with a cellular-connected scale has been a common component of behavioural weight-loss programmes.[1][2] Separate validation work compares consumer-scale body-fat readings against laboratory reference methods such as hydrostatic weighing.[3] Evidence that weight readings from connected scales agree with in-person measurements exists in small samples, whereas the impedance-based body-composition estimates are generally regarded in the validation literature as less precise than the weight figure.[3][4]

paras: A conventional digital scale shows a single weight value on its display. A smart scale adds a wireless link so that each weighing is stored automatically in an app, where graphs and moving averages show change over time. Some research-grade versions are cellular-connected, transmitting readings directly to a study centre without any action from the participant.[2][5]

Many consumer models include metal electrodes in the platform. When the user stands barefoot, a low-level current travels through the lower body, and the device reports an estimate of body-fat percentage, and sometimes muscle mass, water or bone mass, using proprietary prediction equations.

Weight is measured by strain-gauge load cells in the feet of the scale. Studies in weight-management research have compared readings from in-home connected scales with weights taken by staff at in-person visits in samples of adults with overweight or obesity, to test whether home data can substitute for clinic data.[4]

Bioelectrical impedance rests on the principle that water-rich lean tissue conducts current more readily than fat. The device measures resistance and converts it into a body-fat percentage using equations built on reference populations. Because the signal depends on hydration, recent meals, exercise, skin and foot contact and the path the current takes, readings can shift without any change in actual body fat, a limitation commonly noted in guidance on the method.

A 2019 validation study in the journal Health and Technology compared the body-fat reading of a consumer smart scale with hydrostatic (underwater) weighing, a laboratory reference method.[3] Summaries of consumer impedance devices generally report that they track weight well but show larger and less consistent errors for body-fat percentage, so that figures from the two approaches are not interchangeable in absolute terms.

Self-weighing studies address a different question, namely whether frequent weighing supports weight control. A six-month trial of 91 overweight adults tested an intervention built around daily weighing on a cellular-connected scale, a web-based graph and weekly tailored e-mails, against a delayed-treatment control group.[1] A pilot randomised study compared an online commercial weight programme with and without a cellular-connected scale.[2] Another study of 74 adults in a 12-week internet-based programme compared self-reported weights with scale-recorded weights to assess how accurate self-report was.[6]

Impedance scales send a current that is far below the sensation threshold, but manufacturers commonly advise that people with pacemakers or other implanted electronic devices, and pregnant users, avoid them. Day-to-day fluctuation from water, sodium, food and exercise means a single reading may differ from the next without any underlying change; users in physique communities therefore often describe focusing on trends across weeks rather than on individual numbers.

Researchers working on digital health have also noted that daily weighing can be experienced differently by different people. Participants in behavioural programmes generally received structured feedback alongside the scale, so results from those trials reflect the combined programme and not the scale alone.[1][7]

In fitness and appearance-oriented circles the scale is typically discussed as a logging tool, used alongside a tape measure and progress photographs to judge whether a diet phase is producing the intended change in weight and, indirectly, body composition. The body-fat percentage shown by the app is often treated as a relative indicator within one device rather than an absolute value, since different devices report different numbers for the same person.

Most clinical work uses smart scales as part of multi-component behavioural interventions. A 12-month randomised trial in 351 adults with obesity and cardiometabolic conditions in community health centres combined app-based self-monitoring, a smart scale, dietitian calls and clinician counselling; it reported a net weight difference of -4.4 kg versus usual care at six months.[7] Other trials have used connected scales to support daily weighing in weight-loss, maintenance and regain programmes.[1][8][9] These trials test whole programmes, so they do not isolate the effect of the scale itself.
Validation research has compared consumer smart-scale body-fat readings with hydrostatic weighing,[3] and measurement studies have compared in-home smart-scale weights with in-person weights.[4]
